summary:
Climate Doppelgänger is an interactive web application that helps users discover geographically distant places with similar climates or similar patterns of environmental change. Using authentic NASA POWER/MERRA-2 temperature and precipitation estimates for ten locations from 1991–2024, it separates two questions: Climate Twins compares average conditions and seasonal characteristics, while Change Twins compares estimated trends and year-to-year variability.
The project addresses “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” through interactive maps, historical charts, adjustable comparisons, trend magnitudes, confidence intervals and statistical significance assessments. Users can investigate what is changing, where changes appear and how uncertain the estimates are. For example, Lisbon’s closest sampled match changes from Cape Town to Reykjavík when switching comparison modes at default settings.
Climate Doppelganger makes NASA environmental data accessible for education and exploratory investigation. Its transparent methods and reproducible dataset help users look beyond averages while understanding that similarity does not establish statistical significance, common causation or future predictions.
details:
Climate Doppelganger is an interactive web application that helps people investigate environmental connections between geographically distant places. It separates two questions: which locations have similar average climates, and which locations share similar estimated patterns of environmental change? This distinction allows users to explore connections that comparisons based only on average temperature or rainfall could overlook.

The application uses authentic NASA POWER temperature and precipitation estimates, derived from MERRA-2, for ten curated locations from 1991–2024. These include Vancouver, Langley, Lisbon, Cape Town and Reykjavík. A Python pipeline downloads monthly data, validates units, coordinates, dates and missing values, and preserves source metadata, retrieval timestamps and integrity hashes. Annual temperatures are weighted by calendar days, while precipitation rates are multiplied by month lengths before aggregation. The validated dataset is included with the application, allowing the demonstration to operate without contacting NASA at runtime.

The matching engine supports two complementary modes. Climate Twins compares average temperature, annual precipitation and seasonal characteristics. Change Twins compares temperature and precipitation trend estimates alongside detrended year-to-year variability. Features are standardized across the supported locations and combined using adjustable weights into a transparent mathematical distance. Lower distances indicate closer selected features; the score is not a percentage match or a probability.

Users explore supported locations on an interactive map, adjust historical periods and variable weights, and compare temperature and precipitation histories, anomalies and seasonal cycles. Trend magnitudes, confidence intervals, nominal statistical significance, sample sizes and data completeness provide context for each comparison. A historical timeline displays actual annual values, a discovery feature identifies calculated distant pairs, and downloadable analysis reports preserve comparison settings and provenance. Accessible tables provide another way to inspect chart data.

One reproducible example demonstrates the project’s central idea. At default settings, Lisbon’s closest sampled Climate Twin is Cape Town, with distance 0.188. Switching to Change Twins selects Reykjavík, with distance 0.461, despite a mean-temperature difference of approximately 12.2°C. This comparison includes both estimated trends and variability. Lisbon and Reykjavík’s temperature-trend p-values are approximately 0.137 and 0.324, so neither is nominally significant at the 0.05 threshold. Their similarity establishes neither equal trends nor common causation.

The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL JS, Recharts and Lucide React. Python preprocessing and independent scientific checks use NumPy, pandas and SciPy. Automated verification uses Vitest, React Testing Library, Playwright, axe, Pytest, Ruff and Mypy. OpenAI Codex assisted implementation, tests, documentation and presentation tooling, with its role recorded in the project’s disclosure. The application runs in a modern browser on ordinary consumer hardware and builds as a static website compatible with Cloudflare Pages.

The project’s creative contribution is its integration of climate similarity, change similarity and explicit uncertainty within one explainable exploration experience. Its intended impact is educational: helping students, educators and curious users ask better environmental questions and distinguish similarity from significance, causation and prediction.

Development decisions prioritized reproducibility, accessibility, responsive design, transparent calculations and manageable data requirements. Scientific limitations remain visible: ten points do not provide global coverage, gridded estimates may poorly represent local terrain, annual aggregation hides extremes, and the significance calculations do not correct for temporal autocorrelation or multiple comparisons. Broader coverage, additional variables and more advanced inference are future extensions requiring further validation.
dataRefs: NASA POWER — temperature and precipitation data
NASA MERRA-2 — underlying meteorological source for POWER
